metrics.methodology: Latencies use 512 bounded geometric histogram buckets, starting at 1 microsecond and increasing by 5%; quantiles are nearest-rank bucket upper bounds. The last bucket covers the remaining duration range. All terminal client attempts, successful attempts, and failed attempts have separate histograms. Throughput is completed attempts divided by phase wall-clock seconds. Operations are attributed to the phase in which they start. Redirect counts include only terminal MOVED/ASK errors; redirects handled by the client are not observable here.

write_stages.methodology: Diagnostic SET and WAIT stages are excluded from logical request and pacing counts. SET latency includes routing, pool/connection initialization and handled redirections before its terminal result; WAIT latency covers only an attempted WAIT call on the same physical connection. Logical set_wait latency covers the complete write executor operation. A short integer WAIT reply has policy error class wait_short, distinct from client timeout. No WAIT stage is recorded when it cannot start; integer acknowledgement histograms exclude errors. Latencies use 512 bounded geometric histogram buckets, starting at 1 microsecond and increasing by 5%; quantiles are nearest-rank bucket upper bounds. The last bucket covers the remaining duration range. All terminal client attempts, successful attempts, and failed attempts have separate histograms. Throughput is completed attempts divided by phase wall-clock seconds. Operations are attributed to the phase in which they start. Redirect counts include only terminal MOVED/ASK errors; redirects handled by the client are not observable here.

workload_stats.pacing_methodology: Offered requests are ideal period slots from workload Start until the dispatcher observes Stop or parent cancellation; the first slot occurs after one period. The period is one second divided by the configured aggregate rate, truncated to whole nanoseconds. A central dispatcher offers only the latest due slot over an unbuffered channel; missed slots, busy workers, stopped tokens, and tokens with no eligible operation are dropped, without catch-up requests. Started requests count actual workload SET/GET client calls; completed requests count their terminal metrics attempts. After Stop, offered = started + dropped and started = completed. Validation and service probes are excluded. These global counters are not attributed to phases.
workload_stats.guarantee: Every successful client SET acknowledgement is validated, including writes whose subsequent WAIT returned too few replica acknowledgements or an error. Every write uses a unique immutable key. SET errors are ambiguous outcomes and may have executed; they are excluded from the acknowledged-write guarantee. The WAIT-satisfied subset is reported separately and does not imply disk durability or loss-free failover. Redis asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged writes during failover. This check establishes observed post-experiment readability and value equality, not a durability guarantee.

errors: isolate primary network: injected ambiguous disconnect response
methodology: Fault is a complete bidirectional Docker bridge disconnection of the deterministic primary owning the lowest initial slot. Redis remains running. All peer and published client connectivity is removed; this is not a selective or one-way partition.

The orchestration and action-completion anchors are recorded separately using monotonic runtime durations. isolation_duration is a minimum hold from successful action completion, bounded by the recovery deadline; samples and bounded process probes can extend the hold. Actual restoration timestamps record the observed duration.

During isolation, recovery requires the five surviving nodes to converge on healthy usable slot ownership, the original replica to own the selected primary slots, unchanged unaffected ownership, and successful all-shard SET/GET probes over stable_for. A stable milestone is retained while observation continues until restoration.

Docker exec runs fixed Redis liveness and topology commands independent of the disconnected data plane. PONG and unchanged container PID, start time and Redis run ID prove sampled process survival, not cluster health. Isolation success requires at least one such disconnected observation.

Restoration reconnects only the same owned node to the same owned network with its original private IP and loopback port. Process identity and endpoint identity must remain unchanged. Cancellation uses a fresh bounded restoration attempt before independent cleanup; safe cleanup can directly remove an owned detached node.

After restoration, fresh stability tracking requires all six original identities and endpoints, three healthy primaries with synchronized replicas, the promoted replica retaining shard ownership, former-primary demotion, unchanged unaffected shards, and all-shard client probes. Service recovery, connectivity restoration and replication redundancy have separate evidence.

Poll intervals are delays after sample completion; concurrent views are not atomic snapshots. Probes do not prove continuous availability. Workload metrics include terminal client errors separately from probe results. At most 1200 topology samples and 64 process samples are retained.

Traffic drains before validating every successfully acknowledged immutable SET. Missing, corrupt, unreadable or unverified records prevent full recovery. Error-returning SET outcomes remain ambiguous. No client can write to the disconnected minority, so this experiment does not exercise minority-side write conflicts or establish loss-free asynchronous replication.
